summary: X is charging new users $1 per year, currently tested in New Zealand and the Philippines, to fight bots and spam. X director of engineering Eric Farraro said the fee is only one part of a broader strategy that may include payment, phone and ID verification plus traditional heuristics. Critics such as Matt Mullenweg and Cornell's Aditya Vashistha argue the fee won't stop determined spammers and could widen the digital divide.
one_line: X's $1/year fee is just one part of an anti-bot plan that may add payment, phone and ID verification, while critics doubt its effectiveness.
key_facts: X is charging new users $1 per year, currently live only in test markets New Zealand and the Philippines.
X director of engineering Eric Farraro said the $1 fee is one piece of a larger strategy that may include payment, phone and ID verification alongside traditional heuristics and models.
Farraro said X's goal is "to make it difficult and expensive enough that it's less and less viable" rather than to stop bots outright.
Farraro said the cost for a human or script to create accounts is currently pennies, and raising it to even $1 makes the process much more expensive.
Farraro warned that within years AI will be able to solve CAPTCHAs and generate photos and videos "undetectable by human or AI countermeasures."
Elon Musk said the fee "won't stop bots completely, but it will be 1000x harder to manipulate the platform" and that users can read for free but pay $1/year to write.
Musk made similar comments in a conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last month, saying a small payment is "the only way I can think of to combat vast armies of bots."
WordPress founder Matt Mullenweg argued spammers pay for domains costing more than a dollar per year and may use stolen credit cards and identities, so fees alone won't stop them.
Cornell assistant professor Aditya Vashistha said $1 is not equally affordable in the Philippines and New Zealand, and the paywall would broaden the digital divide.
A Similarweb report this week found X's web traffic and monthly active users on mobile had declined since Musk's acquisition.
Competing platforms include Spill, Bluesky, Pebble, Countersocial, Spoutible, Hive, Mastodon and Meta's Threads, and few of them charge a fee.
WhatsApp charged users a $1 annual fee for years until 2016.
It is unclear whether the $1 fee will be permanent when the policy rolls out to other markets.
